video.title: Assessment when pupils have AI
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — teacher educator, Bangladesh (main character)
Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A staff room. A teacher holds out a phone to Dr Farah: a detector’s result, a red gauge at ‘90% AI’. Beside it, a handwritten draft with crossings-out. Farah looks from the gauge to the draft, frowning.
scenes.animation: The gauge needle swings to 90% (≤ 400 ms); quick push-in on the handwritten draft.
scenes.narration: A teacher showed me a detector’s verdict on an essay: ninety per cent AI. The pupil had written every word herself, in English, her second language.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: fair assessment when pupils have AI.

scenes.visual: An essay passes under a magnifying glass labelled ‘detector’. Simple, even sentences light up. A big figure appears: over half of the essays by non-native English writers flagged as AI.
scenes.animation: Sentences highlight one by one; the big figure grows in (0.5 s).
scenes.narration: AI-writing detectors don’t find proof. They guess from patterns, like simple, predictable wording. But many people write that way in a second language. In a twenty twenty-three Stanford study, detectors labelled over half the essays by non-native English writers as AI-written.

scenes.visual: A dial with a threshold line. As the line moves down to catch more cheating, more honest pupils’ essays turn red. One pupil’s face falls.
scenes.animation: The threshold slides down; red flags pop on essays one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: A false alarm is an accusation
scenes.narration: A detector is like any alarm: above some score, it calls the work AI. Set it to catch more cheating, and it accuses more honest pupils. A false accusation can hurt a pupil for years. So a detector score is never proof, and never the judge.

scenes.visual: A task sheet redesigns itself: a plan and two drafts clip on; a speech bubble for talking about the work; a village map pin; a classroom desk with paper.
scenes.animation: Each part clips onto the task sheet as it is said.
scenes.narration: Instead of policing, redesign the task so the learning shows. Ask for the process: a plan, drafts and notes. Add talk: pupils explain their work aloud. Make it local and personal, like interviewing a grandparent. And do key parts in class, on paper.

scenes.visual: A clean white card with the AI track chip. A ladder of four levels, 0 to 3, each with an icon; under it, a short note card a pupil fills in.
scenes.animation: Levels light up one by one, 300 ms apart; the note card slides up last.
scenes.on_screen_text: An AI level for every task
scenes.narration: Then give each task an AI-use level. Level zero: no AI. Level one: AI for ideas only. Level two: feedback on the pupil’s own draft. Level three: AI allowed, if pupils show how. Pupils add a note: which tool, what they asked, what they changed.

scenes.visual: A maths exercise book: on the left page only an answer, ‘x = 7’, with a question mark; on the right page, the same answer with every step of the working, and a teacher’s tick beside a small slip in step two.
scenes.animation: Steps write themselves line by line (1.5 s).
scenes.narration: It’s like “show your working” in maths. A right answer alone could be copied. The working shows what the pupil can really do, and where they need help.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor pops in holding a phone with the detector’s ‘90% AI’ gauge, eyebrows raised. Three answer cards drop in below him.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A detector says a pupil’s essay is ninety per cent AI. What should you do next?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Talk with the pupil about it’ gets a blue check badge. A teacher and a pupil sit side by side over the essay and a page of notes; the pupil points and explains.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); speech bubbles alternate.
scenes.narration: Talk with the pupil about it. Ask them to explain a paragraph, or show notes and drafts. A second detector is just another guess, and a zero could punish an honest writer.

scenes.visual: Two task cards side by side. Before: ‘Write an essay on floods’, with a chatbot finishing it in a blink. After: a pupil interviewing an elder under a tree, drafting at a desk in class, then explaining to a partner.
scenes.animation: The before card fades to grey; the after card builds in three parts.
scenes.narration: Here’s a redesign. Before: “Write an essay on floods”, which a chatbot does in seconds. After: interview an elder about local floods, draft in class, then explain one choice to a partner. AI level one: ideas only.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the Mistakes and thresholds lab: dots for real smoke and cooking steam along a score line, a dashed threshold, and a table of caught, missed and false alarms. The threshold moves right; false alarms drop to zero and the missed count climbs.
scenes.animation: The threshold slides right (1.5 s); counts tick over.
scenes.narration: In the app, you’ll set thresholds for a smoke alarm and a spam filter. Push false alarms to zero, and most real cases slip through. Now picture a detector, where every false alarm is an honest pupil accused.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside a board that reads ‘Homework: a report on our local market’. Three answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: How can he see the learning?
scenes.narration: Your turn. Mr Okafor sets a take-home report on the local market. How can he see the learning?

scenes.visual: The ‘Add a short talk about it’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four points for fair assessment.
scenes.animation: Points tick in, 250 ms apart; the takeaway bar slides up.
scenes.narration: Add a short talk: when pupils explain, you see the learning. Remember: detectors aren’t proof, and they flag second-language writers more. Show the process, set an AI level per task, and ask how pupils used it.

scenes.visual: A classroom. Pupils sit in pairs, one explaining an exercise-book page, the other asking ‘why?’. A two-minute sand timer on the desk. Dr Farah walks between the pairs, listening.
scenes.animation: The sand timer turns; speech bubbles pop in pairs.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: “Show your thinking”. In pairs, each pupil explains one step of their homework aloud for two minutes. The partner asks one question: why did you do it that way? Walk round and listen: it tells you more than any detector.

checkpoints.prompt: A detector says an essay is 90% AI. What should you do next?

options.text: Talk with the pupil about it
Run it through a second detector

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a score is not proof. Ask the pupil to explain their work and show their notes or drafts.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a second detector is another guess, and a zero could punish an honest pupil. Talk with the pupil about the work.

checkpoints.prompt: A take-home report on the local market. How can the teacher see the learning?

options.text: Check every report with a detector
Add a short talk about it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — when pupils explain their work aloud, you hear what they understand, whoever helped with the writing.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — detectors can’t be the judge, and nobody can check a ban at home. A short talk shows the learning.
